teaser: Legend says this boy was painted in blue to win an argument. The dates say otherwise.
review_notes:
Reynolds legend: his remarks on warm and cold colors are in the Eighth Discourse, delivered in 1778; the painting was shown at the Royal Academy in 1770.
Sitter: traditional identification as Jonathan Buttall (son of a hardware merchant, early owner); alternative proposal Gainsborough Dupont, the painter's nephew. Stated as unresolved.
X-rays: abandoned portrait of an older man under the paint; a white dog painted out at lower right and covered with rocks.
Costume described as a studio prop that Gainsborough kept: generally accepted, check.
Gainsborough's habit of using very long brushes and thin paint.
Sale in 1921 by the Duke of Westminster to Henry E. Huntington (through the dealer Duveen) for about $728,000, reported then as a record price.
National Gallery farewell in January 1922: three weeks, about 90,000 visitors; director Charles Holmes wrote 'Au revoir' on the back.
Return loan to the National Gallery opened 25 January 2022, 100 years to the day.
Kehinde Wiley, A Portrait of a Young Gentleman (2021), commissioned by the Huntington: sitter in tie-dye shirt and shorts.
Size about 178 x 112 cm.

lesson.text: The story goes like this. Sir Joshua Reynolds, the most powerful painter in England, declared that blue is a cold color and must never fill the middle of a picture. His rival Thomas Gainsborough heard about it, grinned, and painted a boy in blue from collar to shoe bows, just to prove him wrong.

It is a wonderful story, and the dates ruin it. Gainsborough exhibited the painting in London in 1770. Reynolds gave his lecture about warm and cold colors in 1778, eight years later. If one of them was answering the other, it was not Gainsborough.

So why all that blue? The true hero of this picture had been dead for over a century: Anthony van Dyck, the Flemish painter who made English aristocrats look effortlessly elegant in the 1630s. Gainsborough adored him. The boy's outfit is not the fashion of 1770 at all. It is a costume.

lesson.title: Fancy dress
lesson.text: This suit was about 130 years out of date when Gainsborough painted it. Follow it from the neck down, then come back up to the face.

spots.title: Lace collar
spots.text: A wide lace collar spills over the jacket, straight out of Van Dyck's portraits. Up close it is only flicks and dabs of white: lace suggested without a single thread being drawn.

spots.title: Slashed sleeve
spots.text: The sleeve is cut open to show white linen, a 17th-century luxury. The satin is built from long strokes of blue, slate, turquoise and white laid side by side, never blended smooth.

spots.title: Shoe bows
spots.text: Even the shoes get big blue ribbon rosettes. From head to foot, one color, in a dozen shades.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: After all that dashing brushwork, the face is painted softly and with care. Pink cheeks, lips closed, a level look. He is playing a cavalier, and he knows it.

lesson.text: That quick, streaky handling was Gainsborough's trademark. He liked very long brushes and thin, fluid paint, and he worked on the whole canvas at once so that nothing went stiff. From across a room the strokes fuse into shining satin. One step closer, they fall apart into ribbons of paint.

X-rays show the canvas was secondhand. Gainsborough had begun a portrait of an older man on it, gave up, and painted the boy on top. He also painted a fluffy white dog at the boy's feet, then changed his mind and buried it under a pile of rocks.

A reused canvas suggests that nobody ordered this picture. Gainsborough earned his living flattering paying clients in the spa town of Bath, and he seems to have made this one for himself, to show London what he could do. Which brings up a second legend: who is the boy?

For two hundred years the answer was Jonathan Buttall, son of a rich hardware merchant, who did own the picture early on. Many specialists now doubt it and suggest the painter's nephew and assistant, Gainsborough Dupont. No record settles it. Whoever he is, he poses like a prince, and one prop completes the act, half swallowed by the dusk.
He has politely taken off his hat. Where is it?

spots.title: The plumed hat
spots.text: A wide black hat, nearly invisible against the dark landscape, given away by its white plume. Hat in hand, fist on hip: this is how gentlemen stand in Van Dyck's portraits of the English court.

lesson.text: Hat low, elbow out, stormy sky behind: every signal says nobility, though the model was most likely a tradesman's son or a nephew. In a society obsessed with rank, Gainsborough shows that grandeur can be put on like a suit. The canvas is 1.78 meters tall (about 5 ft 10 in), so the boy meets you nearly life-size.

In 1921 the Duke of Westminster sold the picture to the American railroad magnate Henry E. Huntington for about $728,000, reported at the time as the highest price ever paid for a painting. British newspapers treated the sale as a national loss.

Before it sailed, the National Gallery in London hung it for three weeks, and some 90,000 people came to say goodbye. The gallery's director wrote two words on the back: “Au revoir.” Then the painting crossed the Atlantic and a continent to California, where it has lived ever since.
The Blue Boy is a portrait in disguise: a painting of 1770 dressed as one from the 1630s, made by an artist showing how much a brush can do with a single color.

“Au revoir” means “until we meet again,” and it took a while. In January 2022, one hundred years to the day after the farewell, the painting returned to the National Gallery for a short visit. A few months earlier the Huntington had hung a reply across the room: Kehinde Wiley's portrait of a young Black man in the same pose, in a tie-dye shirt and shorts.

quiz.question: Why can the Reynolds legend not be true?
options: The painting was shown eight years before Reynolds's lecture
quiz.explanation: The picture was exhibited in 1770 and the lecture came in 1778.

quiz.question: Whose portraits inspired the boy's costume?
quiz.explanation: The suit copies the fashion of Van Dyck's sitters from the 1630s.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal at the boy's feet?
options: A white dog, later painted out
quiz.explanation: Gainsborough painted a dog and then covered it with rocks.

quiz.question: Where has the painting lived since the 1920s?
quiz.explanation: Henry E. Huntington bought it in 1921 and took it to California.

quiz.question: What did the National Gallery's director write on the back in 1922?
quiz.explanation: It means “until we meet again,” and the painting did come back for a visit in 2022.

facts.text: The boy wears the everyday fashion of 1770.
facts.explanation: His suit is a costume in the style of the 1630s, about 130 years older.

facts.text: Gainsborough painted The Blue Boy on a canvas he had already used.
facts.explanation: X-rays show an abandoned portrait of an older man underneath.

facts.text: We know for certain that the model was Jonathan Buttall.
facts.explanation: That was the traditional answer, but specialists now doubt it and no record settles it.
